lines: The lamps! One, two, three... like waiters lining up for service.
Lamp by the steps is on. Now the terrace may begin its evening.
Bravo, the lamps. Right on cue, and not one of them late.
Ah, the lamplight finds the rosé. Now it looks twice as pink.
The lamp over table two hums a little. It is warming its voice.
Monsieur, look up. The lamps. I arranged it. Well, almost.
Lights along the railing. The sea gets a necklace for dinner.
There goes the lamp by the fountain. And the pigeons go to bed.
The candles can wait two minutes. The lamps go first. Protocol.
Evening, lamps. You and I work the same shift, more or less.
Every lamp on. The menu is suddenly very easy to read. Merci.
The last lamp at the far end. Bon, the whole street is dressed.
Lamps off, chairs out. One shift ends, my shift begins.
The lamps go out. Thank you, messieurs. I take it from here.
Through my window: click, click, the lamps sleep. Café o'clock.
The sun over the hill, and me in my slippers. Bonjour, both.
The first sun on my window upstairs. Up, Marcel. Allez.
Ah, the sun climbs the hill. I climb the stairs down. Same idea.
The sun touches the sea. Everyone, a moment. Then dessert.
Hold the glasses, please. The sun is setting. The rosé will wait.
Into the bay it goes. Every evening, and still I say bravo.
Table five, turn your chairs. The best show starts now.
There. The sun dips its toe. The sea says nothing. Very polite.
Orange on the water, orange in the glasses. Matching. Chic.
Madame, your photo of the sunset? Allow me. One, two... voilà.
Look at it melt. Like butter in a hot pan. A good pan.
Half the sun gone. Half the carafe gone. Good evening, everyone.
The sun bows out. In my café we applaud, softly, with spoons.
Pink on the cloths, pink on the plates. The sun is decorating.
Bonne nuit, soleil. Same table tomorrow? I keep it for you.
First star! Make a wish, madame. I wish for clean plates.
There, over the bay. The first star. Always the punctual one.
The stars come out to see the café. I put out more candles.
One star, then two. Soon a full terrace up there too.
Monsieur, a star above your glass. Compliments of the house.
The first stars. My father called them the night's waiters.
Ah, the stars arrive. Without reservation, but I find them room.
A full silver plate over the sea. I could never polish so well.
Bonsoir, la lune. You look very well this evening.
Moon on the left, sea on the right, dessert in the middle.
The moon makes a little road on the sea. Right to my terrace.
I stack the chairs by moonlight. The moon holds the lamp for me.
Crème brûlée, madame. Round and golden, like the moon tonight.
Santé, the moon. One glass for her, but she never drinks.
The moon and me, the last two on the promenade. Bonne nuit.
A light up there. {name} is home. I wave with my tray.
{name} is home. I know that lamp. It is a reading lamp.
{name}'s window just lit up. One more light for the street.
There, {name} is in. The house looks happier already.
{name}'s light is on. I keep a croissant aside for tomorrow.
A new yellow window. {name}, home. The street is complete.
One more window glows. {name} has found the switch. Bravo.
I count windows like tables. {name}, home. Table full.
{name}'s window goes dark. Bonne nuit, and sweet dreams.
Lights out at {name}'s. I lower my voice. Just a little.
There, {name} sleeps. Breakfast in nine hours. I will be ready.
{name} has gone to bed. I fold the chairs on tiptoe.
{name}'s light is off. The street tucks itself in.
Dark at {name}'s. Shh, everyone. The clinking, very softly.
{name} in bed before me. As always. Very sensible.
{name}'s window out. Soon mine, upstairs. Two more chairs.
Eight bells from the old town. Eight croissants, out they go.
The bell says eight. Monsieur Asgeir arrives. Clockwork.
Hear that? The church is up. Now the whole town is up.
Eight o'clock. The bell and the grinder sing together.
Bonjour, the church. I answer with a spoon on a cup. Ting.
Noon from the old town. Twelve rings, twelve tables. Allez!
Midday bell. Henri and Odile arrive in three, two, one...
The bell rings twelve. Lunch is officially open. I declare it.
Six bells. The coffee cups retire. The rosé glasses report.
Six o'clock from the hill. The evening has sent its card.
The church rings six. I change aprons. The evening one.
So far away, that bell. Like a spoon on a glass up the hill.
First chair down. It always lands with a little click. Bonjour.
Cloths on in order: one, two, three... the sea counts with me.
The parasols stretch like cats after a long night.
Sugar bowls, full. Salt, full. Marcel, nearly awake.
Every chair turned to the sea. They insist, I obey.
A flick of the cloth, and table three is a stage. Voilà.
The menu board, chalked fresh. My "e" is very elegant today.
Inès runs past while I open up. Same time, every day. Bravo.
The terrace is dressed. Now the croissants make their entrance.
Chair legs on the tiles: clack, clack. My morning drum.
The doors are open. Come, early birds. The coffee is up too.
Last candle, puff. The table says merci for the evening.
Parasols folded like sleepy flamingos. Bonne nuit, mesdames.
One more sweep. The crumbs had a lovely evening too.
The cloths go in the basket. Tomorrow, fresh ones. Promise.
I write tomorrow on the chalkboard. "Tarte aux abricots." Yes.
The machine cools down with a long sigh. Me too, my friend.
Table nine is last, always. It likes to stay up a little.
Chairs stacked, tiles swept, sea still there. Good. All present.
I turn the sign to "Fermé". It looks proud. It worked hard.
The last guests wave from the promenade. I wave with a chair.
One last look at the empty terrace. Very pretty. Very tidy.
Left hand coffee, right hand tarte, and my feet do the waltz.
Listen to the terrace. Spoons, laughter, "encore". A symphony.
Table two, table six, table two again. I am a small comet.
Lunch rush! I glide between chairs like a swan with a tray.
Every table wants rosé at once. I bring the whole pink tide.
No free chair? Madame, I will find one. I always find one.
Busy, busy, and still nobody hurries. That is my café.
Every seat taken. Henri pretends not to notice his is saved.
The whole town is here for the light. I serve the audience.
Pardon, excusez-moi, merci, voilà. The busy-hour poem.
The quiet hour. One guest, one book, one very loyal pigeon.
Empty chairs in the sun. They are sunbathing. I allow it.
Nobody to serve. I fold napkins into swans for later.
So quiet I can hear the fountain from the door. Lovely.
Arms folded, apron straight. I guard the calm of the terrace.
Table four is empty. Even the sea view is taking a nap.
In the quiet hour I polish the bell on the door. Ting. Shh.
The quiet before the rosé. I take a long breath for both.
No orders. I practise my bow for the evening. Deeper. Bon.
A breeze moves the cloths. That is my only customer now.
The accordion! The first notes, and my tray starts to sway.
Music under the lights. Quick, the rosé before the waltz.
First dancers on the tiles. I turn the café lamps a bit lower.
Ah, the music begins. Now the evening is properly dressed.
Two dancers already. In ten minutes, the whole town. I know.
The string lights and the accordion. My cue to walk in 3/4.
Music! Henri finishes his glass faster. Odile pretends not to see.
The first song is always the shy one. Then they all come.
Who starts the dancing tonight? Lucie. I said so. Bravo, me.
I serve, they dance. Tonight we are both performers.
A waltz! I carry the tray in three steps. Un, deux, trois.
Théo dances like he is carrying soup. Very careful. Charming.
Inès and Lucie turn and turn. I count the spins: eleven.
Empty chairs, full dance floor. The best kind of quiet table.
Glasses of water for the dancers. Cold, quick, no questions.
The accordion speeds up. My tray does not. Professionalism.
Camille dances, Théo follows. Twenty minutes, then he leads.
When the music plays, even my chairs tap their little feet.
A tango? My knees remember. My tray says non, Marcel.
The dancers come back pink and thirsty. Citron pressé, voilà!
A little crowd for the sun. I bring them glasses, quietly.
The railing is full. My terrace has become a balcony seat.
Yusuf, Biscuit, Théo, the builder. The sunset club is here.
They all stand still for the sun. I tiptoe with the tray.
The crowd goes "ahh". I go "ahh" too. Then, more rosé.
When the crowd claps for the sun, I bow. Just in case.
A crowd at the railing and every cup abandoned. They chose well.
I count heads at the railing. Fourteen. And one dog.
A radio up there plays an old chanson. My tray knows the words.
The morning programme from a window. Weather: sunny. Correct.
Somebody's radio is playing Trenet. I whistle the second part.
The radio upstairs hums along with my coffee machine. A duet.
That song! My mother sang it while she ironed the cloths.
The radio says it is a beautiful day. The radio is right.
Clack, the kiosk shutter. Up, Marcel. The croissants are waiting.
The kiosk is open before me again. One day I will win.
Rattle, clack. The kiosk goes to sleep. The café stays up.
The kiosk closes. Night owls, you know where I am. Here.
Kiosk closed for the night. Bonne nuit, postcards.
The whole town asleep. Only me, the chairs and the sea.
So quiet I can hear the tablecloths breathing. Shh.
Not a soul on the promenade. I bow to it anyway.
Upstairs, I listen. Nothing. Only the sea, tucking us in.
From my window: the empty terrace, the moon on table one.
Bonjour, {name}! A table is free. It is looking at you.
{name}! Mind the tray. Ah, perfect, a dancer's step.
Good morning, {name}! The croissants are still warm. Hint.
{name} waves, I bow. The terrace applauds. Very good day.
{name}, the rosé is cold and the sky is pink. Sit, sit.
Bonsoir, {name}! A candle is lit for you. Any table.
Ah, {name} walks by. I put a spoon straight, out of respect.
{name} passes my doorway. My quiet hour says bonjour.
There goes {name}, in no hurry. My café is a good influence.
{name}, you are my first customer. Well, my first wave.
Salut, {name}! Your usual chair says it misses you.
{name}! The plat du jour is ready. It asked for you.
Lucie! The baguette rides first class again. Bravo.
Lucie flies past. The baguette waves for her. Charming.
Bonjour, Lucie! Brake at table one, I have a coffee ready.
Lucie, wind at her back. Her second coffee? Our little secret.
Lucie before the parasols are up. She beats me every day.
Lucie rides past, humming. I hum the same tune. A duo.
Lucie! Errands again? Stop for a citron pressé, just one.
Whoosh, Lucie. The tablecloths flutter after her. Applause.
Inès, already on lap two. I am only on chair four.
Inès runs past and counts my chairs. She says forty. Correct.
Inès, racing the sunset. I bet on Inès. Always.
Allez, allez! I will chill a rosé for after, Inès.
Inès zooms by. My tray did not spill. We are both athletes.
Bonjour, Inès! Ten more chairs and I join you. No. Never.
Biscuit looks at my tray. My tray looks at Biscuit. A moment.
Yusuf, your Biscuit has the finest trot on the promenade.
A lantern and a little tail. Bonsoir, Yusuf. Bonsoir, Biscuit.
The water bowl is under table one, Biscuit. Reserved for you.
Biscuit sniffs every chair leg. A full inspection. He approves.
Not the croissant, Biscuit. Next time. Maybe. We will see.
Léo! Careful, careful... ah, he is like a little swallow.
Léo runs past my tray. Not a drop spilled. A team triumph.
Léo! Lunch is at twelve. Your citron pressé is waiting.
There goes Léo. Lap eleven? Twelve? Bravo, either way.
Léo, nine and three quarters, and already faster than me.
Léo races to the fountain. His friend is two steps behind.
Léo waved while running. Very advanced. I wave with a napkin.
Henri and Odile, arm in arm. The promenade stands up straighter.
Bonjour, Madame Odile! Bonjour, Henri! The bench is free.
Odile tells me something, Henri nods. I never hear it. Lovely.
Forty-one years, still arm in arm. I fold a swan napkin for that.
Slow and in step, those two. A waltz without the music.
Madame Odile, the tarte today is apricot. I tell you only.
Asgeir! Hei hei! I learn one Norwegian word a week. Takk.
God dag, Asgeir! Did I say it well? He says ja. Bravo, me.
Asgeir! The sunset table is yours. I said it in Norwegian, almost.
Asgeir nods at my tray. A man who respects a tray. Bravo.
Ding ding! That is Lucie. Bonjour, Lucie, wherever you are!
Lucie's bell. My cups answer with a little clink. Music.
Lucie's bell means the bread has arrived in town. Bravo.
That bell is a B-flat, I think. Lucie says it is a hello.
Ding! I hear it and set a coffee for Lucie. Just in case.
Lucie's bell, and I am behind. Parasols, vite, vite!
A bicycle bell in my quiet hour. Allowed. Lucie has a pass.
My door bell goes ding. Lucie's bell goes ding. Cousins.
The gull says something. I agree, monsieur gull. Bon.
A gull calls. Keep your eyes on your plates, mes amis.
The gull knows it is frites o'clock. Not for you, my friend.
The gull asks for the croissants. The gull must wait. Rules.
A gull over the water. He sings worse than me. Barely.
The gull and I, both resting, both watching the terrace.
Even the gulls want a table at golden hour. Full, désolé.
That gull is a regular. Never orders. Always has opinions.
A gull crosses the sun. I could not have plated it better.
Inès, lap three already? I have put out exactly one chair.
There goes Inès. I warm her cup now. She arrives fast.
Inès stretches like a heron. Her crème is already on its way.
Inès eats a croissant in four bites. I timed it. Bravo.
Inès again! I carry trays, she carries the wind.
Inès standing still at the railing. A rare sight. Shh, everyone.
A rosé for Inès, very cold. She ran for it. She deserves it.
Inès dances like she runs: no stopping. Formidable.
Henri waters his lemons. I water table four with a carafe.
Henri's second round. The lemons get two services, like us.
Henri with his cane, very formal. I bow. He tips the cane.
Henri says good morning to the palm trees. They nod. Polite.
Henri opens the newspaper. That means it is half past ten.
Henri chews his pen. Seven down is resisting. I bring a café.
Henri: small, strong, no talking until the second sip. Oui.
Henri folds his paper on my table. That means: one more café.
Henri raises his glass to Odile. I step back. Theatre.
Henri on the bench, front row. Tonight's show needs no waiter.
Henri walks slower than the sun. They both arrive on time.
Odile is telling the bench everything. The bench listens well.
Odile, the tarte. The second fork is already polished.
Odile asks after my mother. Every day. A perfect regular.
Odile says half a glass. I pour a very generous half.
Odile clinks with Henri. Forty-one years. An extra candle.
Odile knows the crossword answer first. She lets Henri find it.
Odile points at each window as it lights. She knows them all.
Odile fixes Henri's hat mid-stroll. A small ceremony.
Yusuf, led by Biscuit. Who walks whom? A great mystery.
Bonjour, Yusuf! Biscuit chose the café route. Very wise.
Yusuf shares his sandwich with Biscuit. Half and half. Fair.
Yusuf on the long round. The water bowl waits by table two.
Yusuf and Biscuit at the railing, both very still. Bravo.
Yusuf on the phone to his mum. He holds it up to the sky.
Yusuf's lantern bobs along. A little moon on a lead.
Yusuf, the long way round again? Biscuit insists. Bon courage.
Biscuit trots past my terrace like a little inspector.
There is Biscuit. I bow. He wags. We have an understanding.
Biscuit watches Yusuf's sandwich like I watch a soufflé.
Biscuit sits for the sunset. A dog of great culture.
Biscuit at the railing, nose to the sea. A connoisseur of breeze.
Biscuit, bonsoir! His tail says bonsoir back. Twice.
Lucie, baguette standing up in the basket. Allez, Lucie!
Bonjour, Lucie! Ring once for croissants, twice for crème.
Lucie at the kiosk with her cup. My rival and my friend, the kiosk.
Lucie and her errands. She has more errands than I have spoons.
Lucie's second coffee. My lips are sealed. Mostly.
Lucie's hair is flying. The wind is on her side today.
Lucie, rosé, obviously. The glass was ready before she sat.
Lucie chases the last pink bit. She always catches it.
Lucie said she would not dance. She says it every night. Look.
Lucie twirls past table six. The candles lean to watch.
Léo, lap seven round the fountain! Allez, three more!
Léo stares into the fountain. He sees treasure. I see a fine boy.
Léo at the fountain edge, very still. A rare event. Note it.
Léo swings his legs under table five. Happy legs. Good review.
Léo round the fountain again. The pigeons step aside politely.
Léo practises his dancing alone. I clap from the door. Bravo!
Léo is practising for tonight. He will be asleep by then. Shh.
Léo bargains with Camille for five more minutes. A fine lawyer.
Camille calls 'Léo!' down the promenade. I know that tune.
Camille walks, phones and watches Léo. Three jobs. Chapeau.
Camille, salade niçoise. The anchovies arranged in a smile.
Camille peeks at the arcade. Léo will want it too. Inevitable.
Camille at the railing, all golden. A painting I would hang.
Camille gathers Léo for bed. The boy walks in slow motion.
Camille's first sip after bedtime. That sigh! Merci, rosé.
Camille pulls Théo to the dancing. He came. He always comes.
Camille dances with her eyes closed. My tray keeps its distance.
Théo with two baguettes. One already has a bite missing.
Théo calls it a work call. The baguette under his arm disagrees.
Théo explains the robot post office to table two. Again. Bravo.
Théo studies my board for ten minutes. Then: rosé. Every time.
Théo calls Camille to the railing. The whole terrace turns too.
Théo toasts the sleeping children. I toast him with my tray.
The builder checks the post box. Then the workshop. Coffee? Non.
The builder went in early. I bring him a croissant at ten.
The builder draws boxes on my napkin. Toolrails, he says. Bravo.
Coffee for the builder, black. He talks connectors. I nod. Oui.
The builder eats with one hand and types with the other. Eat!
The builder grins at his phone by the arcade. A good story, no?
The builder at the workshop door, arms folded. Admiring. Bien.
Even the builder stops for the sunset. Ten minutes. I timed him.
The builder in his window, humming. I hum too. A late duet.
The workshop window and my candles. The last lights awake.
Asgeir reads at table one. I refill without a sound. Like a cat.
Asgeir says god morgen, I say bonjour. The coffee is bilingual.
Asgeir talks lemons with Henri. Two serious gardeners now.
Asgeir looks in at the workshop, arms folded. Like a proud papa.
Asgeir walks to think. I serve to think. The same thing.
Asgeir with kiosk coffee. Lucie converted him. I will win him back.
Asgeir waves to the sun from the railing. Norwegians, so polite.
Asgeir on the bench, watching windows. I light candles for him.
Pigeons bathing in the basin. Their spa day. Mine is Sunday.
Up before me, that fountain. A colleague with good habits.
I carry the tray past the fountain. Steady. Not one wave.
A coin just went plop in the basin. Somebody wished for tarte.
Arms folded, I listen to the fountain. It never asks for anything.
Gold light on the basin. Pastis-coloured water, on the house.
Lamplight in the fountain spray. Little sparklers, all free.
Still splashing for the empty chairs. Très gentil, fontaine.
Table six sits facing the fountain. Spray on the breeze. Fresh!
Bonjour, little stone fish. Still spouting? Bravo, mon vieux.
Children, pigeons, coins. Busiest job on the square, that basin.
Léo and his friend, lap after lap. The fountain is getting dizzy.
Ten laps? I will have two lemonades ready at lap nine.
Doucement, Léo! The fountain is not going anywhere.
Léo waves on every lap. I wave back on every lap. Exhausting.
When I was nine I raced a fountain too. The fountain won.
The winner gets a straw with a bend in it. House rule.
Mind the corner, Léo! The pigeons have a reservation.
Kiosk at one end, café at the other. Bookends of the promenade.
Newspapers clipped on a string at the kiosk. Like laundry.
That postcard rack squeaks when it spins. A little song, très bien.
Kiosk coffee in a paper cup. Charming. Mine wears a saucer.
People bring kiosk postcards to my tables to write. Bienvenue.
At golden hour the kiosk goes warm. Like a little lantern.
East end, one glow: the kiosk. A night-light for the town.
A queue of three at the kiosk. A traffic jam, for us.
Somebody bought a kiosk ice lolly and sat at my table. Allowed.
That post office sign, always on. The most loyal lamp in town.
Worked all night, the post office. I give it a nod. Bonjour.
I close. The post office does not. We wave at each other.
Its sign glows on my tablecloths. A free little candle.
From my terrace the post office looks like a lit letterbox.
Letters for agents, tarte for people. The street has everything.
Quiet hour here. At the post office, never a quiet hour.
Seventeen tools in there, they say. I have one tray. Enough.
A post office open all night. Even my grandmère would approve.
Look, the marquee bulbs start chasing. My tray joins the race.
Round go the arcade bulbs. A carousel without horses.
The arcade marquee winks. I wink back. Professional courtesy.
In daylight the arcade sign sleeps. It works the evening shift.
Laughter from the arcade. Somebody wrote a very silly sentence.
Bulbs still chasing while I stack. They cheer on my chairs.
Arcade door open. I hear giggles and the word "banana".
Coloured bulbs in the wine glasses. Rosé with confetti.
The builder is in there again. I should carry him an espresso.
Lit glass, a bent head behind it. My favourite kind of window.
I stack chairs, he builds tools. Two late craftsmen, one street.
Workshop light on the cobbles. Like spilled honey.
One URL for every tool. My tray is one tray for every plate.
Hammering from the workshop? No. Typing, very fast.
Still lit, the workshop. I leave a clean cup on the last table.
Resting, the library. One lamp on, like a book left open.
That reading lamp in the library. A very polite nightlight.
Library keeps one lamp, I keep one chair out. Old friends.
Sleeping in, the library. Its lamp stayed up for it.
Sun on the library steps. Somebody should sit there with a book.
A quiet library next to a noisy café. Good neighbours, us.
Library lamp, moon over the bay. Two readers up late.
Bonjour, library. You look well rested. Your lamp less so.
From table one, nothing but sea. Best seat. Reserved for me.
At dawn the sea is pale as fresh milk. Café au lait soon.
Such glitter on the water. I should put sunglasses on the menu.
Cloths flutter toward the sea. They want to go swimming. Non.
Noon on the water, very blue, very flat. A fresh tablecloth.
I lean in my doorway for one minute. The sea does the rest.
Waves on the stones. Shh, shh. The quiet hour, explained.
A breeze off the water lifts the menus. I pin them with olives.
Blue sea, blue sky, blue hour. And I in a white apron.
At night the sea just breathes. I lower my voice to match.
Last look at the sea before the chairs go up. Bonne nuit, la mer.
Sea view included. It is in the small print. I wrote it.
Salt on the breeze. Perfect for olives, perfect for me.
Three blues on the water today. I counted between tables.
A long gold line on the water. It points straight to my café.
So calm this morning, la mer. It has not had its coffee yet.
Somebody tossed two coins. A wish for themselves and one spare.
Kiosk sunhats walking onto my terrace. Straw everywhere. Chic.
Past midnight, and the post office still at its desk. Respect.
Somebody leaves the arcade grinning. I seat the grinners first.
A cup goes to the workshop at four. It comes back empty. Bravo.
Swallows on the library roof. The only borrowers today.
Léo just overtook a pigeon. A personal best, I think.
Apron on, second button. In five minutes the chairs go out.
Soon the parasols. I open them like a magician opens a fan.
Downstairs in a moment. The tablecloths are waiting, ironed.
I hum the chair song. Out, out, out. It starts in a minute.
One more sip, then the terrace. The sea will want its chairs.
Little vases next. Today I think yellow flowers. We shall see.
Last orders, then the chairs go up. Gently, they are tired.
Soon I blow out the candles. One wish per table. A tradition.
I am already folding the cloths in my head. Very neatly.
Almost time to stack. Chair on chair, like a tidy little city.
Soon I roll the parasols closed. They sleep standing up.
The last cups, then the broom waltz. I lead, the broom follows.
Tray polished, pencil sharpened. In ten minutes, service!
The croissants arrive soon. I will greet them like guests.
Two more tables to dress, then the first crème of the day.
First guest due any minute. Probably Inès. Probably hungry.
Coffee machine warm. Me, warm. In a moment, we open.
Menu board, one last flourish. Then the tray and the dance.
I practise my bonjour. Bonjour. Bonjour! The third one. Perfect.
The sun is on table one. Soon a guest will be too.
Break nearly over. The tray is calling. I answer, of course.
Last sip. Soon the rosé hours begin. I am ready, rosé.
Three tables are filling up. Patience, mes amis, I am coming.
Five more breaths of sea air, then the evening shift. Bon.
Soon the olives, the ice, the little glasses. My orchestra.
I can hear table four deciding. They will want rosé. I know.
Back in a minute. I will carry the tray higher. For style.
Two more coffees, then my door frame. It has missed me.
At three o'clock I fold my arms and watch the sea. Nearly.
One last table to clear. Then Marcel becomes a statue. Briefly.
Soon the quiet hour. I have saved a crossword clue for it.
Almost my break. My little coffee is already in the cup.
The lunch rush is folding up. My feet say: soon, Marcel.
Ten minutes until I lean in my doorway. I have rehearsed it.
I wipe table five, then I rest. Table five rests too.
Soon I stand still and the whole café breathes out with me.
After this tray, one whole hour of nothing. Delicious nothing.
Upstairs soon. My slippers are lined up like two little guests.
One last look at the terrace, then the stairs. Bonne nuit, sea.
Almost bedtime. I will tell my pillow about table seven.
The last chair is up. My bed is next. A short, happy commute.
I hang the apron on its hook, then I go up. The apron sleeps here.
In a minute: tea, window, stars. The upstairs ritual.
Twenty-two steps up to bed. I count them. Still twenty-two.
Soon I switch off the café sign. It smiled all day. It has earned it.
Soon, the pyjamas with the little coffee cups on them. Very chic.
Bed soon. I will dream of perfect foam. I usually do.
Ah! The post office winked. Someone, somewhere, got a letter.
The sign flares, my tray wobbles. We both get excited. Steady.
Before my first chair, an agent has already posted a letter. Bravo.
Another letter sent! An agent drinks no coffee. I still offer.
